articles.headline: France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
keyFacts: The French government estimated 320,000 mostly young people protested nationwide on Saturday over living costs and education.
Students and labor unions led the demonstrations, while related youth protests also occurred in Germany, Portugal, and Italy.
Paris police barred nighttime entry to central areas and enforced a nine p.m. curfew for unaccompanied minors.
body: France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
PARIS — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.

France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.
Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.

The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.
The marchers' grievances are diverse.
Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."

The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.

Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.
Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.
Police impose curfew and other measures

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.
Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.

Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.

In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

articles.headline: Mamdani claims Abdul El-Sayed is victim of ‘blatantly racist attacks’ while defending lefty Dem
keyFacts: Mayor Zohran Mamdani claimed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has admirably handled blatantly racist attacks during his campaign.
President Donald Trump and Republican candidate Mike Rogers have attacked El-Sayed over alleged family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.
Senator Ted Cruz criticized a 2011 research paper authored by El-Sayed that warned Arab women about the risks of interethnic mating.
body: Lefty Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed — who has authored research papers advising Arab women not to breed outside their ethnic group – has “admirably” handled alleged racism that’s come his way, Mayor Zohran Mamdani claimed this week.

The socialist mayor praised the way El-Sayed is “navigating” his high-profile Senate contest against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), although within hours of the interview El-Sayed was openly feuding with his primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the final stretch of the campaign.

“A race of that magnitude is difficult enough as it is; to have to contend with blatantly racist attacks on a regular basis, and the silence of so many around him in the face of that — that is immensely difficult,” Mamdani told WNYC in an interview Thursday. “And I have had to experience a version of it in our own mayoral race.”

“And I can tell you that you lean on those around you as much as you can. And you struggle every day to ensure that the race is on the terms that you wanted it to be on. And yet, when we are speaking about millions of dollars being spent trafficking in that same racism, it becomes incredibly difficult to both respond to it and continue to move forward. And it’s a challenge that I think he’s rising to admirably,” said Mamdani.

President Trump and Rogers have centered their attacks on El-Sayed’s apparent family tie to the Muslim Brotherhood, not race. Trump has branded him a “jihadist” and Vice President Vance called him a “psycopath.”

While at Columbia Medical School, El-Sayed — who has repeatedly called himself a physician though he never completed his medical school residency — authored a paper that concluded Arab women should only breed with their own kind for optimal health outcomes.

El-Sayed warned in the 2011 paper published in the “Journal of Immigrant and Minority Health” of the hazards of “interethnic mating” — which he insisted increased the risk of children being born premature.
The paper was one of several he authored that were hyper-focused on race and religion.
“This is ‘science’ with “a pre-ordained racist & eugenics outcome,” Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tx.) wrote on X about El-Sayed’s research. “Scary stuff.”

The mayor was also asked about Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) elevating El-Sayed, who campaigns on Medicare for All and wants to block US aid to Israel. Both Mamdani and El-Sayed have ties to infamous Israel-hating socialist Linda Sarsour.
AOC said a Democratic victory in Michigan would prove “anyone can win anywhere.” But he wouldn’t bite when asked directly whether he wants to see AOC herself run for president.
The New York “Squad” member is touting her nationwide fundraising prowess in a new cash appeal Saturday and could gather steam from socialist wins.
“I want to see AOC do whatever it is that AOC wants to do,” Mamdani said.

articles.headline: Keyboards of The Verge
keyFacts: Staff members at The Verge detailed the specific keyboards they use daily for work and personal computing.
Reported devices include built-in laptop keyboards, Apple Magic Keyboards, and mechanical boards from brands like Keychron and NuPhy.
Several writers noted they may purchase new mechanical keyboards or swap out parts like keycaps and switches in the future.
body: What is a keyboard if not the original brain-computer interface? You can tap on a touchscreen or talk to the computer, but if your work involves getting information out of your head and into the computer, you’re probably spending a lot of time using a keyboard.
Keyboards of The Verge
From the strictly utilitarian to the ergonomic to the obsessive, these are the keyboards we use every day.

We’ve written about many keyboards over the years, from the legendary Optimus Maximus to the ultra-luxe Seneca to even stranger fare. But I wanted to know what my coworkers actually use. As I’d hoped, there’s a wide range. Some of us are strictly utilitarian, optimizing for ergonomics or functionality. Others obsess over every detail of feel, sound, layout, and looks. Still others — maybe the most enlightened — just use whatever’s in front of them.
NuPhy came up a lot. So did Keychron. The Apple Magic Keyboard has its stalwarts. The Kinesis Freestyle split is surprisingly well represented. And there are other, odder entries.
These are the keyboards of The Verge.
Jay Peters, senior reporter

I currently use the Kinesis Freestyle Pro, and I’ve used it for so long that I’ve forgotten when I first got it. In the late 2010s, I had wrist pain that led me to try a lot of ergonomic keyboards so I could keep using computers. The Freestyle Pro — with its optional tenting add-ons that give the keyboard a significant angle and the palm rest accessories — just feels the best under my hands. If this keyboard broke, I’d buy another one the same day.
Kallie Plagge, senior copy editor

For work, I use a simple Keychron K2. But for my gaming PC, I use the Logitech G713 wired mechanical keyboard — the one that comes with the cloud wrist rest. Did I mostly buy it for the wrist rest? Perhaps. But I do love the tenkeyless layout. My previous gaming keyboard had a number pad and two rows of programmable keys, which was cool, but I mostly used the number pad to type the alt code for em dashes. The G713, on the other hand, meets my gaming requirements without taking up half my desk. I’m not playing anything competitive on my PC that requires adjustable actuation points, so the GX red linear switches do the trick. (And they’re the right amount of clicky, unlike the overly loud ones on my K2.) So yeah, maybe I bought it for the sleek all-white look and the cute wrist rest, but it’s also a great keyboard, too.
Danielle Steussy, product manager

I’m using Apple’s Magic Keyboard with the numeric keypad. Some version of Apple’s keyboard has been on my desk for over 20 years, starting with the Apple A1048 that came with my first Mac in college. I loved that keyboard (the sound of my fingertips hitting the keys — swoon!) and I wore it down to the point of keys falling off. Since then, I’ve stuck with Apple’s wireless keyboards. Honestly, it’s a pretty keyboard, but otherwise unremarkable, and blends in with my desk setup (which also is kind of the point, right?). My biggest complaints are that the key legends wear off faster than I’d like and the Bluetooth connection isn’t totally reliable. It’s not my favorite Apple product (by far), but after two decades of muscle memory, I’m not switching anytime soon.
David Pierce, editor at large

I really want to be a mechanical keyboard guy. I love typing on mechanical keyboards! I love the clackiness, the way they look on my desk, the huge personality upgrade that comes with them. But then I start typing notes during a call, and someone goes, “Sorry, what’s that noise in the background?” and I bail on my mechanical keyboard. I used Logitech’s MX Keys S for the last few years, and love that keyboard, but recently replaced it with an Apple Magic Keyboard (black keys, number pad) because I got tired of typing my 1Password password all the time. I bought a $200 keyboard for the Touch ID button. Ugh.
Jacob Kastrenakes, executive editor

My keyboard is probably the single dumbest thing I have ever spent money on, but it brings me joy every time I look at it. The setup matches a Boop Redux case with the GMK Dots keycaps and Silent Bluish White (V2) switches. I didn’t so much want to get deep into the mechanical keyboard hobby as I wanted to have this exact keyboard after I saw images of the Dots keycaps on the (original) Boop case floating around in around 2022. It looks cool, right? (Right?) From a practical standpoint, this is fully a downgrade from the Apple Magic Keyboard I was using before: It’s bigger and louder, with fewer keys, and I probably type a bit slower on it, too, owing to the longer key strokes. It’s also a few hundred dollars more expensive. But you know what? I think it looks really cool.
Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer

Since I review laptops and occasionally mechanical keyboards, I’m constantly changing what I type on. But one of my personal keyboards that remains close to my heart is my TM680 (aka the Gamakay LK67). It’s a cheap bare-bones 65-percent kit I bought from AliExpress in 2021. I was inspired by the video that YouTuber Scott “Keybored” Kim did on it, so I dabbled in modding it.

I started with basic Gateron Milky Yellow linear switches and some crummy knockoff Evangelion keycaps, but I later upgraded to a much nicer MT3 3277 keycap set. I then spent hours individually lubricating and adding switch films to each of the Gaterons, lubing the stabilizers, inserting some foam into the base of the chassis, and adding layers of painter’s tape to the bottom of the PCB. This combination made my basic build sound and feel much better, and it shaped my preference for deeper, “thockier”-sounding boards that I still have today.

My old TM680 is easily outdone by just about any budget board these days. Many switches now arrive pre-lubed from the factory, and even a sub-$100 keyboard can sound and feel nicer right out of the box. But doing the mods myself felt special. I doubt I’ll ever bother with all that work again, because lubing and filming switches is just too tedious and time-consuming, but I’m glad I at least experienced it once. And no matter how many new keyboards I test, I intend on keeping my TM680.
TC Sottek, former senior editor

I used to buy pretty expensive gaming keyboards that I can’t even name now without digging deep through email archives for receipts. I know I once spent nearly $200 on a full-size Razer mechanical keyboard with a numpad that took up a ton of desk space. The key travel felt amazing and it had a great sound. But what I really remember was knocking over a full glass of water on it. Oops! Farewell, keyboard.

Unfortunately, this happened not once, not twice, but three times for me with relatively expensive keyboards over the years. Yes, I should have learned to contain liquids in bottles on my desk. But now I’ve settled for cheap–but–still-good options the same way I’ve done with the several pairs of earbuds I’ve ruined over the years. (Former serial AirPods Pro user here, now fully on board the Nothing Ear train.)

I’m currently rocking a Keychron K2 with a 75-percent layout. It took me a minute to get my 120-plus WPM back on a cramped keyboard, but now it works just fine and I like the look. I’ll probably splurge again someday on a really compelling set of keycaps.
Meredith Haggerty, senior reports editor
I use the laptop that is attached to the M2 MacBook Air I was issued by my employer. It’s right there whenever I need it, but I think they should make a version that’s covered in way fewer crumbs.
Emma Roth, news writer

I have a toxic relationship with my keyboard, a Corsair K55 RGB Pro that I picked up for half the price at a thrift store a few years ago. It’s a decent, budget-friendly keyboard that’s fine to use for gaming and writing. But recently, it’s been getting on my nerves. The keys no longer light up when I turn my computer on, and it sometimes doesn’t sync properly with my Corsair iCUE software. I can’t see what I’m pressing unless the keyboard is lit up (the keys are translucent), so I’ve had to resort to unplugging the keyboard and plugging it back in when I turn on my computer, which usually does the trick. The issue is probably software-related, but I might just get fed up enough to buy myself a fancy new mechanical keyboard.
Andrew J. Hawkins, transportation editor
The latest version of a Verge favorite, this low-profile mechanical keyboard has long battery life, tri-mode wireless, hot-swappable low-profile switches, and remappability.

I have never been a keyboard guy. I was content to use the one attached to my laptop or whatever wireless Apple version I could get for cheap. But I changed when a coworker turned me on to the NuPhy Air75 mechanical keyboard. The keys feel great, the “clack-clack” sound is so satisfying, and the overall design is retro without seeming outdated. That big yellow spacebar, the delightfully orange Enter button, the subtly aquamarine Escape key — chef’s kiss. Connectivity is robust and the battery lasts for days before needing to be recharged. It took some getting used to, but I chalk it up to not being able to use my left ring finger while typing since breaking it in a freak scooter accident years ago. But that’s a different story.
Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor

A 65 percent gasket-mounted wired mechanical keyboard kit. Use the Design Lab to customize its top, bottom, switchplate, and accent colors, plate materials, and mechanical or electrocapacitive PCBs. (Switches, stabilizers, and keycaps sold separately)

These days I mostly swap between a Leopold FC660C and a couple of Omnitype Bauer Lites. The Leopold is a Topre board I’ve had since 2017; I’ve modified it a fair bit over the years, with silencing rings, a new controller board, and Ursa keycaps. I fell in love with the unbeatable tactility of Topre switches early, but I love the customizability of regular mechanical keyboards too, so I’ve spent a lot of time over the past decade trying to find something that combines the best of both.

I got most of the way there with my first Bauer Lite a couple years ago; its Kailh Deep Sea Silent Islet switches are linear, but they’re the closest to Topre I ever found in an MX-compatible switch. (They’re basically identical to the ones in the HHKB Studio). It’s also fluorescent orange, which just makes me happy. I built another one recently with DynaCap electro-capacitive switches and MTNU Space Cadet keycaps. Do I need three wired 65-percent keyboards with very similar layouts and pretty similar typing feel? Probably not. But I have them anyway. Also several other keyboards.
Stevie Bonifield, news writer

I love trying out new mechanical keyboards (and have reviewed dozens of them), but for the last year straight I’ve been using a NuPhy Halo75 V2 as my daily driver. I’ve built several custom mechanical keyboards over the years, but I haven’t changed anything on this one yet. I may swap out the switches and keycaps at some point. NuPhy’s tactile Mint switches are fairly good, but I miss the Leobog Juggle V2 switches I have on a wired keyboard that used to be my daily driver.

I’ve been pretty happy with how the Halo75 sounds and feels out of the box. I also appreciate that the design’s simple enough to not be distracting while still having a few pops of color. The battery life could be a bit better, but there’s not much to complain about overall — the build quality feels solid, the keycaps and switches have held up well over months of heavy typing, and the Halo75 works smoothly with both Mac and Linux. It also has Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless connectivity, which was a must-have for me since I like to hop between multiple devices from the same keyboard.

I’ve had a great experience with the Halo75 so far, but I’d recommend it mainly for Mac users — macOS is where it really shines. It works fine for gaming, but I’d suggest configuring it with linear switches if you want to use it for gaming, rather than the tactile switches I went with.
Brad Bourque, commerce writer

I started building mechanical keyboards a few years ago, and have a few in my quiver, but the one I use most often is a NovelKeys NK65 in white. This 65-percent keyboard is sturdy and compact, with just enough extra buttons for work or surfing the web, and arrow keys in case I want to sneak in some gaming. It’s a hot-swap board, so I change up the setup occasionally, but it’s currently equipped with SA Mizu keycaps and C3Equalz x TKC Dragonfruit tactile switches, with a matching desk pad and metal Escape key.
Adi Robertson, senior tech & policy editor

I’ve upgraded my writing equipment since 2021, when I proudly displayed an Apple Magic Keyboard on top of a piece of cardboard on top of a MacBook with several nonfunctional butterfly keys. And as much as I love collecting dedicated typing machines — I’ve got a Freewrite, a 1990 Smith Corona word processor, a beautiful 1930s Underwood manual typewriter, and an impressively awful faux-vintage one from the zombie-brand era of Royal, among others — I discovered my perfect work setup is low-profile mechanicals: clicky enough to be satisfying, short enough travel to not hamper my typing speed. (I’m still slightly faster on a chiclet keyboard, but I’ll take the hit.) I spent a few years with a NuPhy Air75, but fell victim to its fairly well-known swollen battery issues, so I’ve since switched to the Iqunix MQ80 — which has less of a fun retro color scheme, but a more satisfying heft. I love the idea of giving it a cool custom keycap makeover someday, but for now I’m too cheap and lazy, and perfectly satisfied with its Mirror’s Edge-y sci-fi white.
Sean Hollister, senior editor

Keychrons are the equivalent of Toyotas in the mechanical keyboard world, offering reliability and a great value for the money. The 75-percent V1 Max features RGB backlighting, USB-A and USB-C 2.4GHz dongles, and modifier keycaps for both Windows and Mac. Plus, it offers simple customization that lets you remap any key to your favorite macro command.

I noped out of mechanical keyboards for years because they were too clicky! No good for my shared office space. Then, Verge alum Dan Seifert clued me into the near-silent Boba U4 switches, which I installed in a Keychron V1 (love the small size, love the QMK programmable lighting, love the volume dial!) and I almost never looked back.

I did have to re-spring and lube all the switches to get a familiar level of spring action, which was easy enough. Some of the switches have spontaneously stopped working over the past four years, but it only takes seconds to hot-swap another one in. And a family member bought me 8BitDo’s awesome Nintendo-themed wireless mechanical numpad, so I’m covered there too.
But I don’t think it’s endgame. When I switch back from my laptop, I often miss the faster, more effortless typing I can do on its lower-profile keys. Maybe it’s time for something new.
Robert Hart, AI reporter

I should preface this by saying I know absolutely nothing about keyboards. My standards for what I want are pretty modest: It should work, move easily around my desk, and not hurt my wrists. Looking cool doesn’t hurt.

I’ve cycled through a few over the years, mostly geometric oddities — sorry, ergonomic — like the Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Desktop and Logitech Ergo K860, which were rather unwieldy. I also tried ordering the Kinesis Freestyle Pro Jay uses, but gave up after the supplier tried to pass off clearly damaged kit (read: tangled hair clogging everything) as brand-new.

I’ve been using the Keychron K2 Pro for a few years now. It’s compact, looks great, and holds a charge well. It has no number pad, but that keeps things nimble, and it handily switches between multiple computers I use on the go. There are also fancy lights, though I usually turn them off. The main downsides are having to regularly Google the key commands needed to control it — a pain when those lights won’t stop strobing like a hyperactive Christmas tree. It supports key remapping, so I may attempt a new layout like Dvorak sometime soon.
Elizabeth Lopatto, senior internet typist

First of all, keyboards should be clacky. I want to sound like I am firing a machine gun while I write. Second, due to assorted repetitive stress injuries, my keyboard needs to be split. So I am typing with a light-up gaming keyboard — the lights are optional, I just like them — called the Kinesis Gaming Freestyle Edge RGB. Do I game? Uh, well, I do crossword puzzles. But the Cherry MX Blue switches guarantee I sound fucking productive while I do them.
Nilay Patel, editor-in-chief
Very boring Apple keyboards. Every five years the right side of the spacebar stops working and I buy a new one. Full-size. Numpad for life.

Sky Sports News' Chris Reidy at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium:
"The pressure is continuing to grow on Pierre Sage. Every loss now pushes Steve Parish and Crystal Palace decision-makers closer to making a change.

"Since the 5-0 defeat at Brighton, the powers that be have wanted to see defensive improvements in the team and results pick up. Since then they've lost twice in the Premier League, but at least with some improved performances, notably in cup competitions against Besiktas and Fulham.
"Palace weren't expected to win at Spurs, especially after going down to 10 men, but they're now in the bottom three with Liverpool visiting Selhurst Park next Sunday, live on Sky Sports.
"A vulnerability from set-pieces has been a theme under Sage, which again will be a worry for the hierarchy.

"For the second game running, Palace's away support chanted Sage's name; there's an understanding from them he's been dealt a tough hand after losing Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Munoz in the summer. And the players at Spurs certainly didn't show a lack of effort; in fact, it was the opposite, they put in a shift.
"But this is a results business, as Sage has admitted himself, and Parish hasn't been afraid to make ruthless decisions: think back to Patrick Vieira.

"It feels right that Sage should get fixtures against Coventry and Hull to prove himself, but football isn't always so kind. The performances against Fulham in the Carabao Cup and Tottenham tonight have at least shown fight and resilience.
"It's going to be another interesting few days waiting to see if Parish and co stick or twist."
'A lot more to come from Spurs'
Tottenham defender Jan Paul van Hecke speaking with Sky Sports about De Zerbi and the winning run:
"He's a top manager. I have a really good relationship with him.
"That's a big reason why I came here because he gets the best out of me, and I think there's a lot more to come from us.
"When you win games, the confidence grows. When you keep a clean sheet, that also helps.
"Now we need to stay calm and keep going, and we will win a lot of games for sure."

articles.headline: Trump prosecutions under Biden set precedent for DOJ’s Alaska ‘Decoy Dan’ probe, ex-FEC chair says
keyFacts: The Justice Department is investigating whether Democratic operatives recruited candidate Daniel J. Sullivan to siphon votes from Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
The Justice Department sued Alaska election officials to block certification if Senator Dan Sullivan loses by fewer votes than Daniel J. Sullivan receives.
Former FEC member Hans von Spakovsky argued that the federal prosecution of Donald Trump laid the legal groundwork for this Alaska investigation.
body: The Justice Department is investigating allegations that Democratic operatives recruited Alaska Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan, dubbed "Decoy Dan," to siphon votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan—prompting liberal-leaning election-law experts to accuse the Trump administration of federal overreach.

But former Federal Election Commission member Hans von Spakovsky argued that the Biden-era Justice Department’s prosecution of Donald Trump over alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election laid the groundwork for the Alaska probe.

"The Justice Department has talked about a potential conspiracy to defraud the voters of Alaska and people are saying, 'Oh, he's got no case. That's a weak case,'" Spakovsky, senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. "Well, I suggest you do a Google search and pull up the indictment that Jack Smith got against Donald Trump in the District of Columbia. He set a precedent for this."

Joined by FBI officials and Alaska State Troopers, Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman announced at a Friday press conference that the Justice Department has been investigating whether Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired school teacher who will appear on the ballot without a party affiliation, was colluding with Democratic operatives tied to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign.

The Justice Department previously sued Alaska election officials, seeking to block certification if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses re-election by fewer votes than those cast for Daniel J. Sullivan. The lawsuit was amended Friday to include reporting by The New York Times that the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and senior aides of Peltola's campaign allegedly worked to recruit candidates who could pull votes away from Sen. Sulllivan. Heyman mentioned the Times reporting repeatedly in the press conference.
MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT
"We are taking that extremely seriously," Hetman said.

Sources at the Justice Department told Fox News Thursday that the Trump administration had issued more than 30 subpoeanas in a span of 24 hours as part of its criminal investigation into the alleged collusion, but Heyman did not say at the press conference what criminal charges are being pursued.
"I'm not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not," Heyman said. "That's why we are conducting that thorough investigation."

Von Spakovsky, a former Federal Election Commission commissioner, said potential indictments of Democratic operatives in the Alaska Senate race could rely on federal statutes similar to those Smith, the former special counsel, used in his 2023 indictment of Trump over alleged efforts to overturn the election.

Spakovsky pointed to charges of conspiracy to defraud the United States and conspiracy against rights. In Trump’s case, prosecutors alleged that he used fraud and deceit to obstruct the federal government’s process for certifying the 2020 election and conspired to deprive voters of having their lawful votes counted and honored.

Spakovsky said prosecutors could potentially apply similar theories in Alaska if they determine that Democratic operatives knowingly recruited Daniel J. Sullivan to confuse voters and divert votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME

Smith's "indictment is basically along exactly those same lines, claiming that that Donald Trump was trying to defraud U.S. voters from fair and honest elections. So Jack Smith and Democrats, they set the precedent for the kind of investigation Justice Department is doing now."

Aubrey Wieber, executive director of 907 Initiative, a progressive advocacy group running critical ads against Sen. Sullivan, told Alaska Public Media that the press conference announcing the investigation "on the eve of the election" may be stemming from ulterior motives.
"One could say it appears that they are trying to interfere in an election and put their thumb on the scale," Wieber said.

The Justice Department's lawsuit was filed on Oct. 22, prompting a parade of condemnations from those who argued the federal government had "no authority" to intervene, with many pointing to the Alaska Supreme Court rejecting the state's push to disqualify Daniel J. Sullivan from appearing on the ballot.
GOVERNOR PROBING 'DECOY DAN' SULLIVAN ELECTION SCANDAL WARNS SYSTEM FLAW HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

"DOJ's theory: two candidates named Sullivan might confuse voters. The Alaska Supreme Court settled that in June and the ballot labels the incumbent. DOJ has no role in state election law," Omar Noureldin, senior vice president of policy and litigation at Common Cause of Common Cause, a self-described no-partisan watchdog organization.

Spakovsky called recruiting a candidate with the same name as a political opponent a "dirty trick," but said the recruitment itself was not necessarily a criminal violation. He said the legal analysis could change if operatives paid the candidate or provided services to help organize his campaign.

"The place you run into potential issues is not only if you just recruit a candidate, but you’re being paid to recruit that candidate, and you then provide services to help him run his campaign and organize it," Spakovsky said.

Providing campaign assistance outside of being a volunteer is an in-kind contribution subject to federal reporting and contribution rules. Spakovsky said any failure to properly report such contributions could create a separate campaign-finance violation.

articles.headline: Joe Manganiello Says He 'Will Never Give Up Hope' on His D&D Dragonlance TV Series
keyFacts: Joe Manganiello stated he will never give up hope on producing a live-action Dragonlance TV series and a documentary.
Manganiello said both projects were shelved years ago due to leadership changes and the departure of his supporters at Entertainment One.
Manganiello noted he now has new hope for future collaborations with Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro Digital Games president Dan Ayoub.
body: Joe Manganiello, one of the most famous Dungeons & Dragons players in Hollywood, said he still wants his Dragonlance TV series to come to fruition despite its cancellation several years ago.

The Justice League and One Piece actor was hired as showrunner and screenwriter on the show years ago, promising a live-action adaptation of one of the stories that helped introduce him to tabletop role-playing. After a series of snags, though, Manganiello eventually went on to confirm that his live-action Dragonlance would no longer come to be.

IGN asked Manganiello about his ill-fated D&D project during a conversation at Lucca Comics and Games 2026. He walked us through how, after five years of work, things fell apart, while also teasing that the door for a Dragonlance TV show – and even his documentary – will never close.

"When both of those got put on the shelf due to a change of leadership – due to shuffling going on within [Entertainment One] – those projects became nobody's child," he explained. "I mean, I was hired by Michael Lombardo, who was my old boss at HBO. He hired me to create a television show, to create the next Game of Thrones for him, but then he was gone.

"He's my guy. He's the guy who understood my pitch. He's the one who believed in me. He's the one who saw what it could be, and he's gone. And then, my other producing partner, he was gone, too. So, the two people that I was there with are gone, and the people there had different ideas. All of a sudden, those things become the priority as I'm turning in my script. Now, my people aren't there. Same with the documentary."

Manganiello went on to say that, as his hands-on time in the D&D universe began to fall apart, he had "nobody helping to fight with" him to bring then-in-development projects to life. With Dragonlance officially confirmed to be canned in 2024, it was around this time the actor thought "OK, I'm out," but as he told us, "there is new hope."

"[President of Wizards of the Coast & Hasbro Digital Games] Dan Ayoub is a fantastic leader. He gets it, and we work really well together," he continued. "I think there are talented people within the building now that are doing some amazing things, and we're going to do some amazing things together.

"The dream was always, always to be off running a Dragonlance series, and I will never give up hope on that. And I think there's a lot of people that share that vision. I think the documentary with Danny Ayoub is actually going to be closer to getting out as well."

That's two big updates on two D&D projects that many fans believed were destined to never see the light of day. Still, as the pieces move into place on the board behind the scenes, it's best not to get hopes up too high until Manganiello and the rest of his team have more to announce. For example, Ayoub took up his position as president just four days ago after previously serving as senior vice president of Dungeons & Dragons. It's unclear how this title change may have affected any plans Manganiello mentioned during our interview.

The world of Dungeons & Dragons is trying to come to the live-action world in more ways than one. After a movie adaptation, Honor Among Thieves , launched to critical success and lackluster commercial response in 2023, we've still yet to see a sequel. There is allegedly a second script floating around somewhere , but whether it will leap off the page remains to be seen . For more on Manganiello, you can read about what he had to share from his time working as Deathstroke on Ben Affleck's canceled Batman movie .

articles.headline: Who are the Republicans running without Trump’s endorsement?
keyFacts: President Donald Trump has withheld endorsements from several Republican congressional candidates running in the 2026 midterm elections.
Incumbent Republican Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and David Valadao are running without Trump's endorsement in competitive House toss-up races.
Trump has also declined to endorse Republican candidates in nine solidly Democratic Senate races across the country.
body: President Donald Trump has put in his two cents on most Senate and U.S. House races this year, as Republicans vie to keep their majorities in the upper and lower chambers, but there are several races he has shied away from endorsing.

Trump’s endorsement power in the Republican primary proved effective in ousting some of his least favorite members of the Republican caucuses, including Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) and Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), who each lost their primaries to Trump-endorsed opponents.

But in the general election, with Democratic and Independent voters now in the fold, Trump-endorsed candidates now have the stamp of approval from a president with a new low approval rating , which sits at just 36%, according to an Oct. New York Times /Siena poll.

Several Capitol Hill Republican candidates are running in their general elections without an endorsement from the president. While Trump expectedly left out mostly GOP candidates running in solidly Democratic seats, he has snubbed a select number of toss-up and close-race candidates from his approval.
Here’s the Republicans running in the 2026 midterms without Trump’s endorsement, as of publication time:
House Republicans without Trump’s endorsement

Most of the House Republican candidates Trump has not endorsed are running in deep-blue districts, where the Republican candidates are widely expected to lose on Election Day. However, he has left out some key endorsements from notable House races, ranked toss-ups by Cook Political Report .

One of the most notable House candidates lacking a Trump endorsement is incumbent Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), who is running against Democratic candidate Bob Harvie, the Bucks County Commission Chair. The centrist, four-term congressman has proven himself a difficult candidate for Democrats to beat, retaining his seat since 2019 despite his district voting for former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Joe Biden .

Fitzpatrick’s seat was moved to a toss-up in the forecaster’s rankings four days before election day. Trump has not yet endorsed the congressman, dissing him for often “voting against Trump,” despite House Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-LA) endorsement for the incumbent. Given the district’s pattern of bucking Trump in each of his presidential races, Fitzpatrick has aimed to distance himself from the president as well, voting against the GOP majority in key votes like the final passage of the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act.
While Fitzpatrick led by single digits in the limited polling throughout the race, Harvie recently led by two percentage points in the latest New York Times /Siena poll on the race.

Across the country in California, Trump has also bucked a GOP incumbent from his endorsement in California’s toss-up 22nd congressional district race. Trump has not endorsed incumbent Rep. David Valadao (R-CA) in his toss-up race against Democrat Randy Villegas.

Valadao has purposely distanced himself from the President, voting to impeach him in 2021. After his rebuke, Trump has never endorsed Valadao. The California Republican is, however, endorsed by Johnson.
In 2024, Valadao’s district voted for Trump over Harris by a 5.8 percentage point margin. But California’s Proposition 50 redistricting has given Democrats more of an opening in the district.
In the limited polling on the race, Villegas, a political science professor, has led Valadao.
Villegas heavily leads Valadao in the race’s Kalshi odds, while Harvie currently leads Fitzpatrick in that race’s odds, though they have frequently flipped.
In California, Trump has also left out an endorsement from two other interesting races: California’s sixth and 40th congressional districts.

In the sixth district, former GOP and now independent Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-CA) is running in his redistricted seat against Democrat Richard Pan. Neither Trump nor Johnson has endorsed Kiley, but, according to the Sacramento Bee , Johnson’s PAC has donated heavily to Kiley’s campaign despite his new independent label. Kalshi odds heavily back Pan.
Trump also has not endorsed in California’s solidly Republican 40th district, in which two GOP candidates are facing off against each other.
Senate Republicans without Trump’s endorsement: Blue state challengers

Trump has not yet endorsed in nine of the 35 Senate races occurring in 2026. He has left out endorsements from the Senate races in Colorado, Delaware, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Virginia. Each of the races is ranked as solidly Democratic by election forecasters like Cook Political Report.

In Colorado’s Senate race, Republican candidate Mark Baisley, a Colorado state senator, is taking on incumbent Sen. John Hickenlooper. Baisley is not endorsed by Trump or Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD), but he does hold endorsements from Colorado’s four GOP representatives.

Republican Michael Katz, a former Democratic state senator, has not received an endorsement from Trump or any notable national Republicans in his Delaware Senate race against incumbent Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE).

In Illinois , former state Republican Party chairman Don Tracy is running against Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton (D-IL) to succeed retiring Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL). In the blue stronghold, Stratton leads by double digits in limited polling. Without the Trump endorsement, Tracy has backings from Reps. Mike Bost (R-IL), Darin LaHood (R-IL), and Mary Miller (R-IL).

In Massachusetts and Rhode Island, Republican attorney John Deaton and former Rhode Island Republican Assembly president Raymond McKay, respectively, are running in each northeast state with slim odds of winning. Deaton is challenging incumbent Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), and McKay is challenging incumbent Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI).

New Jersey’s Republican Senate nominee Justin Murphy faces an Everest-like climb against incumbent Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) in the Garden State. Despite his brief moment of virality with his debate answer supporting the Iran war, Murphy has not received an endorsement from Trump or any other prominent national Republican.

In Virginia , GOP Senate candidate Bert Mizusawa , a retired Army major general, is similarly challenging incumbent Sen. Mark Warner (R-VA) on a statewide ballot the year after Virginia Democrats flipped the Governor’s seat blue by a double-digit margin. Mizusawa is endorsed by Rep. Ben Cline (R-VA), but not Trump or popular former Gov. Glenn Youngkin (R-VA).
MEET THE REPUBLICAN SENATE CANDIDATE WHO WANTS TRUMP TO CONTINUE THE IRAN WAR
Oregon’s Republican Senate candidate, GOP State Sen. David Brock Smith, and New Mexico’s Republican Senate candidate, write-in primary winner Larry Marker, are each not endorsed by Trump.
None of the GOP Senate candidates have above a 2.4% chance of winning, according to prediction market Kalshi’s odds.

articles.headline: Celeste and TowerFall have delisted from Xbox's digital storefronts to support BDS boycott
keyFacts: Maddy Makes Games removed Celeste and TowerFall from Xbox digital storefronts.
Maddy Thorson stated on BlueSky that the games were delisted to support the BDS boycott.
The action prevents Microsoft from receiving a cut of sales from these games.
body: Earlier this month, Big Walk developer House House explained why their co-op puzzle adventure wouldn't be available for sale on Xbox: Microsoft's gaming division is a priority target of the the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which names the tech giant in general as a pressure target alongside Google, Amazon, and a host of other companies. House House isn't alone in taking this action.

Narrative platformer Celeste and party fighter TowerFall have delisted from Xbox recently, and Maddy Thorson of Maddy Makes Games fame took to BlueSky to explain why: "For those who’re asking, yes, we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on Xbox. We did this to support the BDS boycott."

For reference, Microsoft gets a cut whenever it makes a sale through its proprietary digital distribution storefront, similar to Steam. Console producers tend to take a loss on hardware, subsidizing it for accessibility to more consumers, so they can make up the difference by selling other stuff, a crucial slice of that other stuff being games.

So as long as sales trickle in for critically acclaimed games like Celeste and TowerFall, that's a bit of easy money for Microsoft—the choice to delist the game stops that. If you're an Xbox owner who wants to observe the boycott, you can always buy used physical versions of games where that's an option or switch to another platform for the time being.

But this is PC Gamer dot com, so you probably haven't even heard of the Xbox. You've certainly never seen one up close. You're probably playing Chessmaster 9000 on your second monitor as you read this, you beautiful freak. In any case, you can always buy TowerFall on Steam. Same goes for Celeste.
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Justin first became enamored with PC gaming when World of Warcraft and Neverwinter Nights 2 rewired his brain as a wide-eyed kid. As time has passed, he's amassed a hefty backlog of retro shooters, CRPGs, and janky '90s esoterica. Whether he's extolling the virtues of Shenmue or troubleshooting some fiddly old MMO, it's hard to get his mind off games with more ambition than scruples. When he's not at his keyboard, he's probably birdwatching or daydreaming about a glorious comeback for real-time with pause combat. Any day now...

articles.headline: Federal judge bars DoJ from threatening election workers to stop processing ballots
keyFacts: A federal judge barred the Justice Department from threatening election workers to stop processing or counting ballots.
Civil rights groups and labor unions sued after the Trump administration demanded California segregate 20,000 ballots over citizenship allegations.
California's midterm election concludes on Tuesday, while officials said processed votes cannot be matched back to voters.
body: A federal judge has barred the justice department from threatening or coercing election workers to stop processing ballots.

The temporary restraining order issued by the US district judge Trina Thompson in the northern district of California late Friday also bars the justice department from demanding local election officials segregate or not count ballots that the federal government deems may have been illegally cast by immigrants, something that is exceedingly rare.
The order came the day after the justice department sent letters to election officials in all 50 states threatening to prosecute and jail any who failed to preserve ballot records.

The justice department’s “intimidation, threats, and attempts at coercion force election workers daily to choose between acceding to defendants’ unlawful demands or adhering to their duties and thereby subjecting themselves to a serious risk of criminal investigation and prosecution”. Thompson wrote.
The order in the lawsuit filed by labor unions and civil rights groups marks another blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over local elections.

It comes after a federal appeals court on Friday rejected the justice department’s request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election, the latest setback for the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over state-run elections.

The administration has alleged California sent ballots to about 20,000 people who may not be US citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are US citizens.
A separate ruling from a three-judge panel on Wednesday forcefully denied that request, warning that the justice department’s demands could disenfranchise citizens.

“As the district court found – and we discern no clear error – there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system,” the ninth circuit court of appeals panel wrote in its 2-1 ruling.
The majority opinion was authored by Judge Mark J. Bennett, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, who was appointed by former Ppresident Joe Biden.

A justice department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling. But in a statement about the sweeping efforts to root out noncitizen voting, it said: “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting. Enforcing that law is not an agenda item. It is the Department’s job.”

Two data scientists from the University of California, Los Angeles recently found that more than 40% of the ballots flagged by the Trump administration bear names that are not even found on the state’s voter rolls, according to the Associated Press. The researchers found that the Trump administration flagged thousands of voters as ineligible, despite the fact that their names corresponded with those of US citizens.

Millions of people have already voted in California in the midterm election that concludes on Tuesday. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. Elections officials have said that processed votes can’t be matched back to the voters who submitted them.
The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli, has said: “Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.”

articles.headline: Ro Khanna Thanks Trump With Verbal One-Two Punch Over His Latest Gripe
keyFacts: Donald Trump criticized Representative Ro Khanna during a Florida rally for receiving airtime on Fox News.
Khanna criticized Trump's war in Iran, claiming it has raised domestic gas and food prices.
Khanna announced that he will appear on Fox News this Sunday to address Trump's foreign policy record.
body: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) delivered a sharp dig at President Donald Trump on Friday after Trump appeared insulted that Fox gave Khanna airtime, telling the president he’ll be back on the network Sunday to comment further on his Iran war “failure.”

“I watch this total dope, Ro Khanna,” Trump said Friday during a midterms rally in Daytona, Florida. “Fox puts him on all the time. You know, Fox is giving Democrats more time than they give Republicans. I don’t know what the hell’s…”

He continued over audible boos at Fox and Khanna, “I’m working my ass off, I’m doing rallies — and I come back and I watch the opponent of the person I did the rally for. I’m not happy. But I watched Ro Khanna, of course, on Fox this morning. I can’t watch him.”
Trump then called Khanna a “radical left loser” over his calls to impeach, claiming Khanna is upset “because I’ve taken the nuclear weapon from Iran.”
Khanna countered with a solid one-two combo, commenting on X under a clip of Trump complaining.

“Thanks for the 4 shoutouts today, Mr. President!” Khanna wrote Friday. “I’ll be on Fox this Sunday to share more of my thoughts on your failure in Iran and how it’s raised gas and food prices. If you get a break from bragging about oil company profits and playing golf, tune in!”

Khanna spearheaded the release of government files connected to late sex offender and former Trump pal Jeffrey Epstein, and has condemned the administration’s continued support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu amid the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Khanna had appeared on “Fox & Friends” mere hours before Trump made his comments, criticizing the Iran war and raising potential impeachment proceedings. He appeared on Fox News last week to warn that the ongoing riots in France are due to global wealth inequality.

Trump is facing disastrous approval ratings amid a nationwide affordability crisis that has only been exacerbated by his war, with several GOP lawmakers and supporters voicing concern that Democrats could win majorities in both the House and Senate in the midterms Tuesday.

Trump on Friday slammed Khanna as a “lightweight” to reporters over his criticisms and defended the estimated $47 billion cost of his war. The California Democrat hit back at that, too, stating on X: “Spend that money on jobs and childcare for Americans.”
He noted, “His voters wanted him to stay out of war. He lied. Result: Blue Tsunami Tuesday.”

articles.headline: Michigan black leader rejects El-Sayed as ‘snake oil’ salesman in undercover video: ‘Just flat-out disdain’
keyFacts: Undercover video shows Michigan activist Charles E. Williams II criticizing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's progressive platform as unrealistic.
A poll found a 16-percentage-point gap between general Democratic support and support for El-Sayed among Black voters in Michigan.
Civil rights leader Al Sharpton rallied Detroit voters to encourage turnout while declining to endorse El-Sayed's candidacy.
body: A black leader in Michigan — who’s been dubbed Al Sharpton’s “little brother in the movement” — is rejecting Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed, blasting the radical candidate as an untrustworthy “snake oil” salesman and saying there’s “flat-out disdain” for him in the community.

Charles E. Williams II, Michigan chapter president of Sharpton’s National Action Network, lambasted El-Sayed’s lack of cultural credibility in undercover footage that lays bare the dilemma facing black leaders torn between their aversion toward El-Sayed — and the community’s expectation they vote blue no matter what.

“You can’t pluck the heart strings of people selling them all of the pie in the sky, that’s not realistic,” Williams said in a video taken outside a meeting at his historic King Solomon Missionary Baptist Church last Saturday and obtained by The Midwesterner.

“You can tell people ‘Medicare for all’ and ‘money out of politics,’ how you going to do it? You ain’t no majorities. You ain’t got no executive branch. You put together legislation and you’re going to send that to Donald Trump, he going to sign that? No!” he exclaimed.
“So you just selling snake oil …. That’s the real issue that I have with the so-called Democratic Socialists and super progressives anyway,” he went on, getting increasingly wound up.
“You selling wolf tickets … You will not get that across.”
Williams acknowledged he did not want El-Sayed to win the Democratic primary.

“I’ve tried to be cordial to the party and make sure they don’t feel like I’m just completely off the farm or anything, but I’m not really happy … I supported the white lady over him!” he said, referring to El-Sayed’s Democratic primary challenger Haley Stevens.
“Him and I have some issues that we have had personally, telling me one thing and then doing another, which is a thing culturally that I have seen, I’ve had to deal with that community,” he added.
Inside the meeting at his West Side Detroit church, Williams made it clear the black community is lukewarm at best towards El-Sayed yet would be shamed for voting Republican.
“I know that there is some hesitancy, some skepticism, and there’s some just flat-out disdain for the person who is the senatorial candidate for the Democratic Party,” he said.

“Let’s be very clear, it ain’t just us. … white folks know how abusive the Arab community have been to not just people in Detroit, they do it all over the place. … so we ain’t the only people who had to struggle with this,” Williams added in the meeting with get-out-the-vote volunteers.
“Sad to have to paint the brush over Abdul but you know, it’s a sticky situation,” he stated.

“I’m educating people to make sure that they go out and vote, but I ain’t going out to tell them to go vote Republican, either,” Williams continued in the video, eliciting multiple “amens” from the crowd. “If they do, that is their prerogative. That is their prerogative.”

“We can’t risk losing the ballot, the entire ballot, because of places where we have some consternation,” he explained, seemingly resigned. “Do what you gotta do. Vote how you gotta — vote how you feel.”
That aversion was on full display Thursday, as El-Sayed spoke at the Historic Second Baptist Church in Benton Harbor.
The crowd that came to hear him — in a neighborhood that is 82% black, according to the latest census — was almost entirely white.
“Crowd looks a bit different,” quipped journalist David Weigel on X.
Sharpton, who trekked to Detroit on Tuesday to meet with Williams and rally get-out-the-vote efforts, stopped short of endorsing El-Sayed.
“It’s not whether we’re Democrat or Republican, it’s that we’re going with who’s best for us,” Sharpton said as he rallied black voters in Detroit.
Reached by phone, he wouldn’t comment on El-Sayed, only saying he was in Michigan to encourage the black community to exercise their right to vote.
